extracted.intended_audience: students learning calculus (advanced high-school or undergraduate) and instructors preparing/using calculus exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, definitions, and recommended rigorous practices for differentiating and integrating elementary functions (powers, quotients, inverse functions, trig, exponentials, logarithms), plus series/limit representations and their conditions of validity. Emphasis on correct hypotheses (continuity, domain restrictions) and method justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial expansion coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of (1 + x)^n as polynomial 1 + a1 x + a2 x^2 + ... + a_n x^n and formula for coefficients a_k = n(n-1)...(n-k+1)/k! (with a_n = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differentiation of (1+x)^n and evaluation at x=0 to identify coefficients; examples and exercises given to prove coefficients for general k by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power rule for differentiation (integer and rational exponents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x^n (n integer) the derivative is n x^{n-1}. More generally, if r is any positive or negative rational number then the function x^r has derivative r x^{r-1} (with domain restrictions when needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine differentiation formulas for integer powers and extend by algebraic manipulation/continuity to rational exponents; when integrating x^r use n ≠ -1 (i.e. r ≠ -1) and if r<0 avoid x=0 by assuming positive limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If q(x) = f(x)/g(x), then q'(x) = (g(x) f'(x) - f(x) g'(x)) / g(x)^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume g(x) ≠ 0 on the region of interest. Proof is an exercise; use to differentiate rational functions and derive derivatives of reciprocal trig functions (e.g., sec, cosec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative of inverse functions (reciprocal derivative)
rubrics_metrics.description: If y=f(x) and x=g(y) are inverse functions, then g'(y) = 1 / f'(x) (or equivalently dx/dy · dy/dx = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be proved from difference-quotient reciprocals or geometrically by interpreting tangents relative to the other axis; use substitution y=... to compute derivatives of explicit inverses (e.g. x^{1/m}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule (compound functions) in Leibniz notation
rubrics_metrics.description: For z = Z(x) = A(y(x)) with y = g(x), dz/dx = (dz/dy)·(dy/dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leibniz notation dz/dy · dy/dx emphasizes cancellation-like manipulation of differentials as useful shorthand, provided one remembers d represents passage-to-the-limit symbolically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leibniz notation: use and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dy/dx and ∫ f(x) dx as compact symbols for limits; treat the symbol d as an indicator of the limiting process, not as a new 'infinitely small' number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leibniz notation is extremely useful (and almost indispensable in advanced theory), but avoid attributing unmathematical literal meaning (true infinitesimals) to d; one may heuristically cancel differentials only as a mnemonic for chain/reciprocal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentials as approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'differential' may legitimately denote a small finite difference Δx when Δx is small relative to other quantities; this is useful for approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse this pragmatic use with the discredited notion of actual infinitesimal numbers; the rigorous foundation is limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (version 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For F(x) = ∫_a^x f(u) du (a fixed lower limit), F'(x) = f(x) provided f is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: differentiation undoes integration. Proof uses bounding the increment by (x1-x)m and (x1-x)M where m and M are min/max of f on the small interval and continuity ensures m,M→f(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive functions and evaluation of definite integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If G'(x)=f(x) (G a primitive function), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = G(b) - G(a); primitives differ by an additive constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the term 'primitive function' to 'indefinite integral' to avoid confusion with definite integrals; determine constant by using F(a)=0 when F(x)=∫_a^x f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity and termwise integration/differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrals and derivatives distribute over finite sums: the integral (or derivative) of a sum is the sum of the integrals (derivatives) of the terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When integrating or differentiating series or sums term-by-term, ensure the hypotheses (continuity/integrability, convergence on interval) that justify termwise operations; examples apply to polynomial and power series terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for integrating power functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) evaluate between limits a and b to get (b^{n+1}-a^{n+1})/(n+1), assuming n ≠ -1. If n < 0 exclude zero from integration interval (assume positive limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly check n ≠ -1 and domain of integrand before applying formula; when r<0 ensure a,b>0 to avoid singularity at zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of derivative of inverse tangent to integrate 1/(1+x^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since d/dx(arctan x) = 1/(1+x^2), ∫_0^b 1/(1+x^2) dx = arctan b - arctan 0 = arctan b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boundary values (e.g., arctan 1 = π/4) to turn integrals into known constants; this yields classical results like Leibniz' π/4 series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termwise integration of a uniformly convergent series (geometric/alternating series example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate the finite geometric/alternating expansion of 1/(1+x^2) term-by-term over [0,1]; the remainder term can be bounded and shown to tend to zero so the infinite series integral converges to the integral of the limit function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly bound the remainder T_n by an integral that tends to zero (e.g., |T_n| < 1/(2n+1)) to justify termwise integration and convergence to π/4; check radius/interval of validity of series (-1<x≤1 here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of natural logarithm via integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Define log x (natural logarithm) by log x = ∫_1^x (1/u) du for x>0; log 1 = 0 and log is continuous and increasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition immediately gives derivative log'(x)=1/x and algebraic properties (log(ab)=log a + log b) via composition and differentiation arguments; exclude x≤0 from domain because integrand has singularity at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of e and exponential as inverse of log
rubrics_metrics.description: Define e as the unique number with log e = 1. Define the exponential E(y) as inverse function of log, so E(log x)=x and E(a)E(b)=E(a+b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend E to real exponents by continuity from rationals; represent a^x generally as e^{x log a}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative of the exponential and general a^x
rubrics_metrics.description: E'(y)=E(y) (the exponential equals its derivative). For f(x)=a^x = e^{x log a}, f'(x)=a^x log a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differentiation of inverse functions and chain rule; special case a=e gives derivative e^x = e^x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit representations of e^z and e
rubrics_metrics.description: e^z = lim_{n→∞} (1 + z/n)^n. In particular e = lim_{n→∞} (1 + 1/n)^n and e^{-1} = lim_{n→∞} (1 - 1/n)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits are bases for deriving series expansions (via binomial theorem) and for continuous compounding examples; apply with care to justify passage to limit termwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-series (Taylor/series) expansion for e^x and error control
rubrics_metrics.description: e^x = Σ_{k=0}^∞ x^k/k! (and in particular e = Σ 1/k!). Truncation error after n terms is bounded by the (n+1)-st term magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive via binomial limit or Taylor series; error bounds given (remainder < next term) provide practical numerical approximation guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit/product expression for logarithm
rubrics_metrics.description: log x = lim_{n→∞} n( x^{1/n} - 1 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from derivative definition and limit h→0 of (log(x+h)-log x)/h; useful representation but not the primary numerical method for log.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series expansion for log(1+x) and region of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: log(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - x^4/4 + ... (alternating series), obtained by integrating geometric series termwise; valid for -1 < x ≤ 1 (x=1 included, x=-1 excluded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express expansion with finite remainder R_n and bound R_n to show it tends to zero as n→∞ on the stated interval; choose interval so denominators 1+u≥1−a with a<1 to bound remainder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic differentiation as a technique
rubrics_metrics.description: For a product P(x)=∏_{i=1}^n f_i(x), differentiate log P(x) = Σ log f_i(x) and obtain P'(x) = P(x) Σ f_i'(x)/f_i(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when differentiating products or expressions like x^{x} or complicated multiplicative forms to simplify the computation; examples provided (e.g., x(x+1)...(x+n), x e^{-x^2}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical modeling: exponential growth/compound interest as limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrete compound interest (w0(1+ r)^t) tends to continuous compounding w0 e^{rt} as compounding frequency increases, via limit (1 + r/n)^{nt} → e^{rt}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limit representations of exponential to pass from discrete to continuous models; can compute doubling times etc. by solving exponential equations.
